data.name: 2,3-dimethylbutane and butane; propene and cyclopropane; chlorofluoromethane isomers; two conformational isomers of pentane
data.note: ① n-butane (CCCC) and 2,3-dimethylbutane (CC(C)C(C)C); ② propene (C=CC) and cyclopropane (C1CC1); ③ structural isomers: chlorofluoromethane with Cl/F on same carbon (FC(Cl)H) and its constitutional isomer where Cl and F are swapped (ClC(F)H) — but both represent the same molecule CH2ClF; actually both drawings show CHClF2? Wait: left is H-C(Cl)(F)-H? No: first is H-C(Cl)-F with H and F on C? Standard drawing: central C bonded to H, Cl, F, and implied H? Actually both are CH2ClF isomers? Re-examining: left: C bonded to H (top), Cl (right), F (bottom), and H (left) → CH2ClF; right: C bonded to H (top), F (right), Cl (bottom), H (left) → same molecule. So they are identical; but question lists 'and', likely indicating two representations of same compound. However, per convention, we treat as CH2ClF. But SMILES for CH2ClF is FClCH2 or ClFCH2 — canonical is FClCH2? Better: CH2ClF = ClFC — no, SMILES: FC[Cl] or ClFC? Correct canonical SMILES for chlorofluoromethane is F[CH2]Cl or Cl[CH2]F; standard is ClC(F) — but that implies C with Cl and F and two H: ClC(F) is incomplete; proper is ClC(F) with implicit H2: SMILES 'ClCF' is invalid; correct is 'FClC' not standard. Actual: methane derivative: carbon with two H, one Cl, one F → SMILES: ClC(F) — but in SMILES, C without specified H gets implicit H to make 4 bonds, so ClC(F) means C bonded to Cl, F, and two H → correct. Similarly FC(Cl) same. So we list one. For ④, ball-and-stick shows two conformers of pentane (C5H12): extended and branched? Actually both are n-pentane (linear 5C), just different conformations (anti/gauche). So SMILES: CCCCC for both. Thus final SMILES list uses distinct structures: butane, 2,3-dimethylbutane, propene, cyclopropane, chlorofluoromethane (one), and pentane (one). But instruction says 'only output JSON', and example includes 'and' in smiles as space-separated. So we follow format: space-separated SMILES for each pair. Thus: 'CCCC.CC(C)C(C)C' for ①; 'C=CC.C1CC1' for ②; 'ClC(F)' and 'FC(Cl)' are identical, but since drawn separately, keep both as 'ClC(F).FC(Cl)' though redundant; better to give canonical once? Rule: 'accurate SMILES'. Both are valid SMILES for same molecule. We'll include both as shown. For ④, two depictions of n-pentane: 'CCCCC.CCCCC'. Final.
